title: Service Mesh
summary: What a sidecar-based mesh adds on top of plain service-to-service calls — mTLS, retries and circuit breaking, and traffic control without touching application code.

slides.markdown:
Once [inter-service-communication](inter-service-communication) is happening between many services, every team ends up reimplementing the same cross-cutting logic: retries, timeouts, encryption, metrics. A **service mesh** moves that logic out of application code and into a shared network layer.

Think of it as a universal translator and bodyguard standing next to every service: it handles encryption, retries, and routing so the service's own code only has to worry about business logic.

slides.sectionTitle: What a service mesh adds on top of plain service-to-service calls
slides.markdown:
Without a mesh, every service that makes a network call has to handle its own retries, timeouts, TLS, and metrics — usually via a shared library, which means every service updates that logic on its own schedule and often drifts (Java services on one retry policy, Python services on another).

A **service mesh** intercepts all service-to-service traffic transparently and applies these policies consistently, in one place, regardless of what language a service is written in. A Python service and a Java service both get the same retry policy, the same mTLS, and the same traffic metrics, without either one importing a shared library.

The trade: you gain consistency and language-independence, and you add a new piece of infrastructure that every request now passes through.

slides.sectionTitle: Sidecar proxy pattern: data plane vs control plane
slides.markdown:
A mesh has two layers. The **data plane** is a lightweight proxy (like Envoy) deployed as a **sidecar** — a second container running alongside every service instance in the same pod — that transparently intercepts all inbound and outbound traffic for that instance. The **control plane** (like Istio's `istiod`) is the brain: it configures every sidecar with routing rules, certificates, and policy, without touching any application code.

Application code still just makes a normal network call to `payments-service`; the sidecar silently intercepts it, applies mTLS, retries, and load-balancing, then forwards it to the destination's sidecar, which does the same in reverse.

This split — dumb, fast proxies doing the work, one smart control plane configuring all of them — is what lets you change a retry policy mesh-wide without redeploying a single service.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: sidecars intercepting all service traffic
slides.markdown:
![Two pods with sidecar proxies talking to each other, configured by a control plane](assets/sidecar-mesh-topology.svg)

Application code never calls another service directly — it always talks to its own sidecar, which talks to the destination's sidecar. The control plane configures every sidecar's routing, certificates, and policy from one place.

This is why a mesh can add mTLS or a new retry policy without a single line of application code changing: the sidecars are the ones doing the work.

slides.sectionTitle: mTLS between services: identity and encryption without app changes
slides.markdown:
**mTLS** (mutual TLS) means both sides of a connection present a certificate, so each service can cryptographically verify the other's identity — not just "this traffic is encrypted" but "this really is the Payments service calling me, not something spoofing its name."

Without a mesh, adding mTLS means every service team integrates a TLS library, manages certificate rotation, and handles handshake failures — real, recurring work multiplied across every service. With a mesh, the sidecars handle the handshake and certificate rotation transparently; application code keeps making plain HTTP calls to a local address, and the sidecar upgrades it to mutual TLS on the wire.

This is often the single most-cited reason large organizations adopt a mesh: encrypting and authenticating all internal traffic without touching hundreds of services' codebases.

slides.sectionTitle: Traffic management: retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, canary routing
slides.markdown:
Beyond security, the mesh's traffic-management layer lets you tune how requests flow without redeploying services. **Retries and timeouts** get set as policy ("retry twice with a 200ms timeout") applied uniformly. **Circuit breaking** stops sending traffic to an instance that's failing, giving it room to recover instead of piling on more load. **Canary routing** sends, say, 5% of production traffic to a new version of a service so you can watch its error rate before shifting everyone over.

The common thread: these are all *policy* changes — edit a config, apply it, watch the sidecars pick it up — rather than code changes requiring a build and deploy of the service itself.

This is what lets a platform team roll out a canary release or tighten a timeout mesh-wide in minutes, instead of waiting on every service team to ship a code change.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: logic in the mesh vs logic in application code
slides.markdown:
| | Logic in the mesh (sidecar) | Logic in application code |
|---|---|---|
| Consistency across services | Uniform — every language, every team gets the same policy | Varies — depends on which library version each service uses |
| Change velocity | Fast — config change, no redeploy | Slower — code change, test, deploy per service |
| What it's good for | Retries, timeouts, mTLS, routing, metrics — cross-cutting network concerns | Business rules, validation, anything tied to what the request *means* |
| Debuggability | An extra hop to reason about — is this failure my code or the sidecar's policy? | Easier to trace — it's all in one process's logs |

**How to decide:** push generic network concerns (retries, encryption, routing) down into the mesh; keep anything that depends on business meaning (should this specific request be retried, what does a 4xx mean here) in application code.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: adopting a service mesh before you have enough services to justify it
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "A service mesh is best practice for microservices, so we should install one as soon as we have more than one service."

**Why it's wrong:** a mesh adds a sidecar to every pod, a control plane to operate and upgrade, and a new failure mode — the sidecar itself can misbehave or add latency. For five services with one team, a shared library handling retries and TLS is far cheaper to run and debug than standing up Istio or Linkerd, and the consistency problem a mesh solves (many teams, many languages drifting on policy) doesn't exist yet.

**Correct model:** reach for a mesh once you have enough services, teams, and languages that policy drift and per-service TLS integration have become a real, recurring cost — not as a default the moment you have more than one deployable.
